brief: Create an 8-slide educational carousel for founder-led B2B SaaS teams showing a practical daily GTM operating system. Adapt the attached dark cheat-sheet poster into a premium editorial system, not a copy: black charcoal background, orange and warm cream typography, thin cream/orange outlines, rounded rectangular panels, terminal/editorial type feel, subtle grain, compact labels, strong hierarchy, and a 2-column card grid where useful. Keep every slide readable on mobile. Cover must show exactly: ULTRON and 51ultron.com. Do not mention or display any other company names. Do not include pricing or dollar amounts anywhere, especially not on the final slide. Final slide must be a comment CTA asking viewers to comment with the GTM task that consumes the most founder time. Use this slide plan: 1) Cover: Founder GTM Cheat Sheet, subtitle: the essential daily workflows for keeping pipeline moving without adding headcount. 2) The operating loop: Signal -> Decide -> Draft -> Ship -> Learn, with one-line explanations. 3) Morning scan: pipeline movement, new prospects, replies, churn signals, content opportunities. 4) Research workflow: identify a narrow account pattern, capture trigger, write one relevant angle, queue the next action. 5) Outreach workflow: context first, one problem, one proof point, one low-friction question, follow-up only when there is a reason. 6) Content workflow: one customer pain becomes a LinkedIn post, X thread, email, and short carousel. 7) Founder control panel: what to review daily, weekly, and monthly, with clear do-not-track noise. 8) Comment CTA: ask viewers to comment the GTM task that steals the most time, with ULTRON and 51ultron.com present but no sales pitch. Tone is direct, practical, systems-minded, and specific to solo founders and small B2B teams.

slots.subtitle: The essential daily workflows for keeping pipeline moving without adding headcount.
slots.coverNote: Built for solo founders and small B2B teams.

slots.body: Treat GTM like a repeatable sequence, not a mood. Each step creates the input for the next one.
slots.p1Body: Notice what changed in the market, the pipeline, or the inbox.
slots.p2Body: Choose the one move that deserves attention now.
slots.p3Body: Create the asset, send it, then refine the next pass.

slots.body: Spend a few minutes on live signals before you write or send anything. This keeps the day tied to reality.
slots.p1Body: Check stalled deals, fresh meetings, and anything advancing.
slots.p2Body: Look for fit, timing, and a clear reason to reach out.
slots.p3Body: Prioritize responses, cancellations, and renewal risk first.

slots.body: Do not research broadly. Pick one account pattern, one trigger, and one angle that makes the next message feel obvious.
slots.p1Body: Write down what changed and why it matters now.
slots.p2Body: Connect the trigger to a concrete problem you solve.
slots.p3Body: End with the exact follow-up you will send next.

slots.body: Lead with context, not a pitch. Keep it specific enough that the recipient knows why you wrote.
slots.p1Body: Name the pain in plain language.
slots.p2Body: Use a single relevant example or result.
slots.p3Body: Ask something easy to answer, then follow up only with a reason.

slots.body: One customer pain can power multiple formats. Reuse the same insight instead of starting over each time.
slots.p1Body: State the pain, the mistake, and the better move.
slots.p2Body: Break the problem into short, fast points.
slots.p3Body: Reuse the same core message in a tighter format.

slots.body: Review the few signals that change decisions. Ignore activity theater and keep the dashboard clean.
slots.p1Body: Check pipeline, replies, and active priorities.
slots.p2Body: Review wins, stalls, patterns, and next actions.
slots.p3Body: Watch trends, not vanity noise or scattered activity.

slots.body: Tell us which GTM task eats the most founder time in your week. Keep it specific and practical.
slots.closingLine: The best systems start with the work you repeat most.
